2.1.goal: Compare the exact probability found by counting outcomes with the relative frequency from a seeded simulation, using the lesson's coins and two dice.

blocks.title: List the sample space of two coins
blocks.text: itertools.product writes out every sequence of two flips, just like the lesson's table. Counting the sequences with exactly one head gives the exact probability, with no guessing.
blocks.code:
from itertools import product

flips = list(product('HT', repeat=2))
one_head = [f for f in flips if f.count('H') == 1]

print('sample space:', flips)
print('exactly one head:', one_head)
print(f'P(exactly one head) = {len(one_head)}/{len(flips)} = {len(one_head) / len(flips):.4f}')

blocks.title: Count the ways to roll a 7
blocks.text: Two dice give 6 x 6 = 36 equally likely pairs. We count the pairs that add to 7 and divide by 36. This exact value is the target the simulation should approach.
blocks.code:
pairs = list(product(range(1, 7), repeat=2))
sevens = [p for p in pairs if sum(p) == 7]
exact = len(sevens) / len(pairs)

print('pairs:', len(pairs))
print('pairs that sum to 7:', len(sevens))
print(f'exact P(sum = 7) = {exact:.4f}')

blocks.title: Simulate rolling two dice
blocks.text: A seeded generator rolls two dice again and again, so the result is the same every time you run it. The relative frequency is (times a 7 came up) divided by (rolls). Watch it settle near the exact value.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

for n in [10, 100, 10_000, 1_000_000]:
    total = rng.integers(1, 7, size=n) + rng.integers(1, 7, size=n)
    freq = (total == 7).mean()
    print(f'{n:>9,} rolls: relative frequency = {freq:.4f}')

print(f'exact value              = {exact:.4f}')

r.code:
pairs <- outer(1:6, 1:6, "+")      # all 36 sums
mean(pairs == 7)                  # exact P(sum = 7)

flips <- expand.grid(c("H", "T"), c("H", "T"))
heads <- (flips$Var1 == "H") + (flips$Var2 == "H")
mean(heads == 1)                  # exact P(exactly one head)

set.seed(42)
n <- 10000
mean(sample(6, n, TRUE) + sample(6, n, TRUE) == 7)
r.expect: 0.1667 (6/36); 0.5; the simulated value is close to 0.1667 (for example 0.16 to 0.17)
r.note: The exact numbers match Python. R's random generator differs from NumPy's, so the simulated frequency is close to 0.1667 but not identical.

spss.menu: Transform > Compute Variable (after the data exist); Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Descriptives
spss.syntax:
INPUT PROGRAM.
LOOP #a = 1 TO 6.
LOOP #b = 1 TO 6.
COMPUTE die1 = #a.
COMPUTE die2 = #b.
END CASE.
END LOOP.
END LOOP.
END FILE.
END INPUT PROGRAM.
COMPUTE seven = (die1 + die2 = 7).
DESCRIPTIVES VARIABLES=seven.
spss.note: The loops write all 36 pairs as 36 rows. A true/false test gives 1 or 0, so the mean of seven is the probability, 0.17 (0.1667). SPSS has no one-click simulation menu, so this shows the exact count only.

stata.code:
clear
set obs 36
gen die1 = ceil(_n/6)
gen die2 = mod(_n - 1, 6) + 1
gen seven = (die1 + die2 == 7)
summarize seven

clear
set seed 42
set obs 10000
gen total = ceil(6*runiform()) + ceil(6*runiform())
gen seven = (total == 7)
summarize seven
stata.note: The first summarize gives the exact mean .1666667. The second is a simulation: close to 0.1667 but not identical to Python's, because the generators differ.

try: Change the event from sum = 7 to sum = 2. Predict the exact probability first (how many pairs?), then run it.
Change the seed 42 to 7 in the simulation. Do the small-sample frequencies change? What about the one-million-roll line?

2.2.goal: Count podiums, committees and lottery tickets with factorials, permutations and combinations, and confirm the counts by listing the possibilities.

blocks.title: Factorials
blocks.text: n! is the number of ways to line up n different things. Python's math module has factorial built in. By convention 0! equals 1.

blocks.title: Permutations and combinations
blocks.text: math.perm(n, r) counts ordered selections (a podium of 3 from 8 runners). math.comb(n, r) counts unordered ones (a 3-person committee from 10). Dividing the permutations by r! gives the combinations.
blocks.code:
print('podiums, perm(8, 3)       =', math.perm(8, 3))
print('committees, comb(10, 3)   =', math.comb(10, 3))
print('perm(10, 3) / 3!          =', math.perm(10, 3) // math.factorial(3))
print('poker hands, comb(52, 5)  =', math.comb(52, 5))

blocks.title: List them to confirm
blocks.text: For small cases we can write out every selection with itertools and count it. Choosing 3 of 5 people gives 60 ordered lists but only 10 groups, a ratio of 3! = 6.
blocks.code:
from itertools import permutations, combinations

people = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E']
ordered = list(permutations(people, 3))
groups = list(combinations(people, 3))

print('ordered lists:', len(ordered), ' formula:', math.perm(5, 3))
print('groups:', len(groups), ' formula:', math.comb(5, 3))
print('first groups:', [''.join(g) for g in groups[:4]])

blocks.title: From counting to probability
blocks.text: One lottery ticket wins out of every possible set of 6 numbers from 49. The chance is 1 divided by the number of tickets. The all-hearts hand is (ways to pick 5 hearts) divided by (all hands).
blocks.code:
tickets = math.comb(49, 6)
print(f'tickets = {tickets:,}')
print(f'P(jackpot) = {1 / tickets:.2e}')

hearts = math.comb(13, 5) / math.comb(52, 5)
print(f'P(5 hearts) = {math.comb(13, 5)} / {math.comb(52, 5):,} = {hearts:.4f}')

r.code:
factorial(4)                 # 4!
choose(10, 3)                # committees
choose(8, 3) * factorial(3)  # podiums (permutations)
choose(52, 5)                # poker hands
choose(49, 6)                # lottery tickets
1 / choose(49, 6)
ncol(combn(5, 3))            # lists the 10 groups
choose(13, 5) / choose(52, 5)
r.note: Base R has choose() and factorial() but no permutation function, so we multiply choose(n, r) by factorial(r). Python's value for 5 hearts is 0.0005 (0.000495).

spss.menu: Transform > Compute Variable (use the Arithmetic functions, LNGAMMA is in the list)
spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / dummy.
BEGIN DATA
1
END DATA.
COMPUTE fact4 = RND(EXP(LNGAMMA(5))).
COMPUTE perm83 = RND(EXP(LNGAMMA(9) - LNGAMMA(6))).
COMPUTE comb103 = RND(EXP(LNGAMMA(11) - LNGAMMA(4) - LNGAMMA(8))).
COMPUTE lottery = RND(EXP(LNGAMMA(50) - LNGAMMA(7) - LNGAMMA(44))).
FORMATS fact4 TO lottery (F10.0).
LIST VARIABLES=fact4 perm83 comb103 lottery.
spss.note: SPSS has no built-in factorial or combination menu item. The closest honest route is LNGAMMA, because LNGAMMA(n + 1) is the log of n!. We turn it back with EXP and round, which gives 24, 336, 120 and 13983816.

stata.code:
display factorial(4)
display comb(10, 3)
display comb(8, 3) * factorial(3)
display comb(52, 5)
display %12.0f comb(49, 6)
display 1/comb(49, 6)
display comb(13, 5)/comb(52, 5)
stata.note: Stata's comb(n, k) and factorial() match Python; there is no permutation function, so podiums are comb(8, 3) times 3!. The %12.0f format stops the big lottery number from showing in scientific notation.

try: How many 4-person committees can be chosen from 10 people? Predict whether it is more or fewer than 120, then run it.
Change the 3 in permutations(people, 3) to 2. Predict both counts, then check the formulas.

2.3.goal: Check the addition rule (heart or king) and the multiplication rule for independent events (heads and a 6) by exact counting and by simulation.

blocks.title: Build a deck and count
blocks.text: We number the 52 cards 0 to 51: the first 13 numbers are hearts, and the last card in each group of 13 is a king. Counting gives the pieces of the addition rule, including the king of hearts that is counted twice.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

cards = np.arange(52)
heart = cards // 13 == 0
king = cards % 13 == 12

print('hearts:', heart.sum(), ' kings:', king.sum(), ' both:', (heart & king).sum())
print('heart or king, counted directly:', (heart | king).sum(), 'of 52')

blocks.title: The addition rule
blocks.text: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). Subtracting the overlap fixes the double count, and the answer matches the direct count.
blocks.code:
p_heart = heart.mean()
p_king = king.mean()
p_both = (heart & king).mean()

print(f'P(heart) + P(king) = {p_heart + p_king:.4f}  (too big)')
print(f'minus overlap {p_both:.4f}   = {p_heart + p_king - p_both:.4f}')
print(f'direct count 16/52    = {(heart | king).mean():.4f}')

blocks.title: Check the addition rule by simulation
blocks.text: Now we really draw cards, one at a time with replacement, using a seeded generator. The share of draws that are a heart or a king should land close to 16/52.
blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
draws = rng.integers(0, 52, size=200_000)

sim_or = ((draws // 13 == 0) | (draws % 13 == 12)).mean()
print(f'simulated P(heart or king) = {sim_or:.4f}')
print(f'exact 16/52                = {16 / 52:.4f}')

blocks.title: The multiplication rule
blocks.text: A coin and a die do not affect each other, so the events are independent and P(heads and 6) = 1/2 x 1/6. We flip and roll 200,000 times and count how often both happen.
blocks.code:
coin = rng.integers(0, 2, size=200_000)
die = rng.integers(1, 7, size=200_000)

both = ((coin == 1) & (die == 6)).mean()
print(f'simulated P(heads and 6) = {both:.4f}')
print(f'1/2 x 1/6                = {0.5 * 1 / 6:.4f}')
print(f'P(heads) x P(6) in sample = {(coin == 1).mean() * (die == 6).mean():.4f}')

r.code:
card <- 0:51
heart <- card %/% 13 == 0
king  <- card %% 13 == 12
mean(heart) + mean(king) - mean(heart & king)
mean(heart | king)            # direct count

0.5 * 1/6                      # heads and a 6

set.seed(42)
n <- 200000
mean(sample(0:1, n, TRUE) == 1 & sample(6, n, TRUE) == 6)
r.note: The exact numbers match Python. R's simulated frequency for heads and a 6 is close to 0.0833 but not identical, because R and NumPy use different generators.

spss.menu: Transform > Compute Variable; Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Descriptives
spss.syntax:
INPUT PROGRAM.
LOOP #i = 0 TO 51.
COMPUTE card = #i.
END CASE.
END LOOP.
END FILE.
END INPUT PROGRAM.
COMPUTE heart = (TRUNC(card/13) = 0).
COMPUTE king = (MOD(card, 13) = 12).
COMPUTE both = (heart = 1 AND king = 1).
COMPUTE either = (heart = 1 OR king = 1).
DESCRIPTIVES VARIABLES=heart king both either.
spss.note: Each variable is 1 or 0, so its mean is the probability: .25, .08, .02 and .31 (0.3077 for either). Check that .25 + .08 - .02 matches .31. SPSS has no quick simulation menu, so only the exact count is shown.

stata.code:
clear
set obs 52
gen card = _n - 1
gen heart = floor(card/13) == 0
gen king = mod(card, 13) == 12
gen either = heart | king
summarize heart king either
display 0.5 * 1/6

clear
set seed 42
set obs 200000
gen win = (runiform() < 0.5) & (ceil(6*runiform()) == 6)
summarize win
stata.note: The means .25, .0769231 and .3076923 match Python. The last summarize is a simulation: close to 0.0833 but not identical to Python's.

2.4.goal: Read conditional probabilities from the lesson's table of 200 students (studied or not, passed or not) and show that P(pass given studied) is not P(studied given pass).

blocks.title: Build the two-way table
blocks.text: We list the 200 students as (group, result) pairs, then pandas crosstab counts them into the same table you saw in the lesson. margins=True adds the totals.
blocks.code:
import pandas as pd

rows = ([('Studied', 'Passed')] * 90 + [('Studied', 'Failed')] * 10
        + [('No study', 'Passed')] * 40 + [('No study', 'Failed')] * 60)
df = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=['group', 'result'])

table = pd.crosstab(df['group'], df['result'], margins=True)
print(table)

blocks.title: P(pass given studied), two ways
blocks.text: First restrict to the Studied row and take the share who passed. Then use the formula P(A and B) / P(B). Both routes must agree.
blocks.code:
n = len(df)
studied = table.loc['Studied', 'All']
both = table.loc['Studied', 'Passed']

print(f'row method : {both} / {studied} = {both / studied:.3f}')
print(f'formula     : {both / n:.3f} / {studied / n:.3f} = {(both / n) / (studied / n):.3f}')

blocks.title: The reverse question is different
blocks.text: P(studied given pass) restricts to the Passed column instead. The numbers differ, so never swap the two. Normalising the table by row or by column shows both at once.
blocks.code:
passed = table.loc['All', 'Passed']
print(f'P(pass | studied) = {both / studied:.3f}')
print(f'P(studied | pass) = {both} / {passed} = {both / passed:.3f}')

print('\nrow percentages (condition on the row):')
print(pd.crosstab(df['group'], df['result'], normalize='index').round(3))

r.code:
tab <- matrix(c(90, 10, 40, 60), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
              dimnames = list(c("Studied", "No study"), c("Passed", "Failed")))
addmargins(tab)
tab[1, 1] / sum(tab[1, ])         # P(pass | studied)
tab[1, 1] / sum(tab[, 1])         # P(studied | pass)
prop.table(tab, 1)                # row proportions
r.expect: P(pass | studied) = 0.9; P(studied | pass) = 0.6923; row proportions 0.9 0.1 / 0.4 0.6
r.note: prop.table(tab, 1) divides each row by its total, which is exactly conditioning on the row. Use prop.table(tab, 2) to condition on the column.

2.5.goal: Find the chance of really being sick after a positive test (1% prevalence, 99% sensitivity, 95% specificity), by Bayes' formula and by counting 10,000 people.

blocks.title: The test's numbers
blocks.text: These are the lesson's numbers. Sensitivity is P(positive given sick); the false alarm rate is 1 minus the specificity. Write them down once and reuse them.
blocks.code:
prevalence = 0.01      # P(sick)
sensitivity = 0.99     # P(positive | sick)
specificity = 0.95     # P(negative | healthy)
false_alarm = 1 - specificity

print('P(sick)                =', prevalence)
print('P(positive | sick)     =', sensitivity)
print('P(positive | healthy)  =', round(false_alarm, 2))

blocks.title: Bayes' formula
blocks.text: P(sick | positive) = P(positive | sick) x P(sick) / P(positive), where P(positive) adds up both ways of testing positive: sick people and healthy people with a false alarm.
blocks.code:
p_pos = sensitivity * prevalence + false_alarm * (1 - prevalence)
ppv = sensitivity * prevalence / p_pos

print(f'P(positive)         = {p_pos:.4f}')
print(f'P(sick | positive)  = {ppv:.4f}')

blocks.title: Check with 10,000 people
blocks.text: Count people instead of multiplying probabilities. Of 10,000 people, 100 are sick, and 5% of the 9,900 healthy people get a false positive. Only the positives matter for the question.
blocks.code:
people = 10_000
sick = round(people * prevalence)
healthy = people - sick

true_pos = round(sick * sensitivity)
false_pos = round(healthy * false_alarm)

print('sick:', sick, ' healthy:', healthy)
print('true positives:', true_pos, ' false positives:', false_pos)
print(f'{true_pos} / {true_pos + false_pos} = {true_pos / (true_pos + false_pos):.4f}')

blocks.title: Why the prior matters
blocks.text: Keep the same test and change only how common the disease is. The same positive result means very different things for a rare and a common disease.

r.code:
prev <- 0.01; sens <- 0.99; spec <- 0.95
p_pos <- sens * prev + (1 - spec) * (1 - prev)
sens * prev / p_pos                 # Bayes' formula

sick <- 10000 * prev                 # 100
true_pos  <- sick * sens             # 99
false_pos <- (10000 - sick) * (1 - spec)   # 495
true_pos / (true_pos + false_pos)
r.expect: P(positive) = 0.0594; P(sick | positive) = 0.1667 both ways (99 of 594)
r.note: Both routes give 0.1667, about 16.7%, the same as Python.

spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / dummy.
BEGIN DATA
1
END DATA.
COMPUTE p_pos = 0.99*0.01 + 0.05*0.99.
COMPUTE ppv = 0.99*0.01 / p_pos.
COMPUTE true_pos = 10000*0.01*0.99.
COMPUTE false_pos = 10000*0.99*0.05.
COMPUTE ppv_counts = true_pos / (true_pos + false_pos).
FORMATS p_pos ppv ppv_counts (F8.4).
LIST VARIABLES=p_pos ppv true_pos false_pos ppv_counts.
spss.note: SPSS has no Bayes menu, so we use Compute Variable on one row. Expect 0.0594, 0.1667, 99, 495 and 0.1667.

stata.code:
display "P(positive) = " (0.99*0.01 + 0.05*0.99)
display "Bayes: " (0.99*0.01 / (0.99*0.01 + 0.05*0.99))
display "true positives: " (10000*0.01*0.99)
display "false positives: " (10000*0.99*0.05)
display "counts: " (99 / (99 + 495))
stata.note: display works as a calculator. Stata prints .0594 and .1666667 without a leading zero; these are the same as Python's 0.0594 and 0.1667.

2.6.goal: Compute expected values for a die and for roulette, then watch the running average of simulated die rolls settle on 3.5 (the Law of Large Numbers).

blocks.title: Expected value of a die
blocks.text: E(X) is each outcome times its probability, added up. A die never shows 3.5, but 3.5 is where the average of many rolls ends up.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

x = np.arange(1, 7)
p = np.full(6, 1 / 6)

print('x * P(x):', (x * p).round(4))
print('E(X) =', round((x * p).sum(), 4))

blocks.title: Is a bet worth taking?
blocks.text: A $1 roulette bet on one number wins $35 with probability 1/38 and loses $1 otherwise. A negative expected value means a long-run loss for the player: the house edge.
blocks.code:
win, lose = 35, -1
p_win = 1 / 38

ev = win * p_win + lose * (1 - p_win)
print(f'expected gain per $1 bet = {ev:.4f}')
print(f'that is a loss of about {abs(ev) * 100:.1f} cents per dollar')

blocks.title: Simulate and track the running average
blocks.text: We roll a die 5,000 times with a seeded generator. The running average after n rolls is the cumulative total divided by n. Early values jump around, later ones stay near 3.5.
blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, size=5000)
running = np.cumsum(rolls) / np.arange(1, 5001)

for n in [5, 50, 500, 5000]:
    print(f'after {n:>4} rolls: average = {running[n - 1]:.3f}')

blocks.title: Draw the running average
blocks.text: The line wobbles wildly at first and then flattens onto the expected value. Individual rolls stay random; the average becomes predictable.
blocks.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.4))
plt.plot(np.arange(1, 5001), running, color='#2563eb', lw=1.2)
plt.axhline(3.5, color='#dc2626', ls='--', label='E(X) = 3.5')
plt.xscale('log')
plt.xlabel('number of rolls (log scale)')
plt.ylabel('running average')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

r.code:
x <- 1:6
sum(x * 1/6)                  # E(X) of a die
35 * (1/38) + (-1) * (37/38)  # roulette

set.seed(42)
rolls <- sample(6, 5000, replace = TRUE)
cumsum(rolls)[c(5, 50, 500, 5000)] / c(5, 50, 500, 5000)
r.expect: 3.5; -0.0526; running averages close to 3.5 by 5000 rolls (not identical to Python's)
r.note: The two expected values are exact and match Python. R draws different random rolls, so its running averages are close to 3.5 but not the same as Python's.

spss.menu: Transform > Compute Variable (expected values); Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Descriptives (the simulated mean)
spss.syntax:
SET SEED=42.
INPUT PROGRAM.
LOOP #i = 1 TO 5000.
COMPUTE roll = TRUNC(RV.UNIFORM(1, 7)).
END CASE.
END LOOP.
END FILE.
END INPUT PROGRAM.
DESCRIPTIVES VARIABLES=roll.
COMPUTE ev_die = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6.
COMPUTE roulette = 35/38 - 37/38.
FORMATS ev_die roulette (F8.4).
LIST VARIABLES=ev_die roulette /CASES=FROM 1 TO 1.
spss.note: Exact: 3.5 and -0.0526. The simulated mean of roll is close to 3.5 but not identical to Python's, and SPSS has no menu for a running-average plot.

stata.code:
display (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6
display 35/38 - 37/38

clear
set seed 42
set obs 5000
gen roll = ceil(6*runiform())
gen running = sum(roll) / _n
list running in 5
list running in 5000
summarize roll
stata.note: The two display lines are exact (3.5 and -.0526316). In Stata sum() is a running total, so dividing by _n gives the running average. The simulated values are close to 3.5 but differ from Python's.

try: Change the random seed from 42 to 1. Does the early part of the curve change? Does the end?
Replace the die with a roulette bet (+35 with probability 1/38, otherwise -1) and predict where the running average heads.
